question:
Circles \(\omega_1,\) \(\omega_2,\) and \(\omega_3\) each have radius \(4\) and are placed in the plane so that each circle is externally tangent to the other two. Points \(P_1,\) \(P_2,\) and \(P_3\) lie on \(\omega_1,\) \(\omega_2,\) and \(\omega_3,\) respectively, so that \(P_1P_2=P_2P_3=P_3P_1\) and line \(P_iP_{i+1}\) is tangent to \(\omega_i\) for each \(i=1,\) \(2,\) \(3,\) where \(P_4=P_1.\) See the figure below. The area of \(\triangle P_1P_2P_3\) can be written in the form \(\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b},\) where \(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers. What is \(a+b?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2018_AMC_12B_Q25_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Joining the circle centers gives known lengths, while the tangent radii supply right angles. These two observations let us determine the triangle's side length.

[Figure 1](figures/2018_AMC_12B_Q25_question_fig1.svg)

Let \(O_i\) be the center of \(\omega_i\), and let \(s>0\) be the common side length of the equilateral triangle. External tangency gives \(O_1O_2=O_2O_3=O_3O_1=8\). Also, \(O_iP_i=4\), and each radius \(O_iP_i\) is perpendicular to its designated tangent line \(P_iP_{i+1}\).

We must account for which side of each tangent line contains its circle's center. Define \(\varepsilon_i=1\) if \(O_i\) is on the same side of \(P_iP_{i+1}\) as the triangle's third vertex, and define \(\varepsilon_i=-1\) otherwise.

View \(P_1P_2\) horizontally, with \(P_1\) to the left and \(P_3\) above it. The radius perpendicular to \(P_2P_3\) makes a \(30^\circ\) angle with the horizontal. Its vertical component has magnitude \(4/2=2\), and its horizontal component has magnitude \(\sqrt{4^2-2^2}=2\sqrt3\). Thus \(O_1\) is \(4\varepsilon_1\) units above \(P_1\), while \(O_2\) is \(2\varepsilon_2\) units below \(P_2\) and has horizontal displacement \(2\sqrt3\varepsilon_2\) toward \(P_1\). The Pythagorean theorem therefore gives
\[
64=(s-2\sqrt3\varepsilon_2)^2+(4\varepsilon_1+2\varepsilon_2)^2.
\]
The same calculation applies to each cyclic pair of centers.

If the three signs were not all equal, two would have a common sign \(t\), and the remaining one would have sign \(-t\). Of the two cyclic pairs ending at a center with sign \(t\), one starts at another center with sign \(t\), while the other starts at the center with sign \(-t\). Their horizontal terms in the displayed equation would be identical, but their vertical terms would have magnitudes 6 and 2. Their squared distances would differ by \(36-4=32\), contradicting that both distances are 8. Hence all three signs equal some \(t\in\{1,-1\}\).

The length equation now becomes
\[
(s-2\sqrt3t)^2=28,
\qquad s=2\sqrt3t\pm2\sqrt7.
\]
Because \(s>0\) and \(\sqrt7>\sqrt3\), only the plus sign before \(2\sqrt7\) is possible. Thus
\[
s=2(\sqrt7+t\sqrt3).
\]
An equilateral triangle of side \(s\) has height \(\sqrt3s/2\), so its area is
\[
K=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2
=10\sqrt3+6t\sqrt7.
\]
The choice \(t=-1\) gives the smaller positive area. It satisfies
\[
10\sqrt3-6\sqrt7
=\frac{48}{10\sqrt3+6\sqrt7}<2,
\]
since both \(\sqrt3\) and \(\sqrt7\) exceed \(3/2\), making the denominator greater than 24. But \(\sqrt a+\sqrt b\ge2\) for positive integers \(a,b\). The stated form of the area therefore selects \(t=1\), giving
\[
K=10\sqrt3+6\sqrt7
=\sqrt{300}+\sqrt{252}.
\]
To verify that another representation cannot change the requested sum, put \(n=a+b\). Squaring \(\sqrt a+\sqrt b=K\) gives
\[
2\sqrt{ab}=552-n+120\sqrt{21}.
\]
On squaring again, every term except \(240(552-n)\sqrt{21}\) is an integer. Since \(\sqrt{21}\) is irrational, this forces \(n=552\). Therefore \(a+b=\boxed{552}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
